paper_title: GameRealm: Grounding Visual Learning in Interactive Games

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.

To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence. 1. Introduction The pursuit of physical intelligence requires visual foundation models to understand not only the appearance of the world, but also its underlying geometry, dynamics, and interactions. Developing such capabilities demands large-scale, diverse, and richly supervised visual experiences. Modern video games offer compelling source of such data, combining visually rich environments, complex scene dynamics, and interactive behaviors. More importantly, game engines provide direct access to precise, game-native supervision, including metric depth, camera poses, and motion information (Li et al., 2026b), which remains difficult to acquire accurately and at scale in the real world. This unique combination of visual diversity, interactive dynamics, and geometric precision positions game environments as powerful foundation for advancing visual intelligence. Despite growing demands for large-scale visual data, existing datasets remain fragmented across tasks and supervision modalities. Interactive world models require temporally aligned visual observations, control inputs, and audio to learn action-conditioned dynamics, whereas geometric foundation models depend on accurate depth, camera poses, and stereo or multi-view observations for 3D/4D reconstruction (Wang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026). However, as summarized in Tab. 1, existing datasets rarely satisfy these requirements simultaneously. Conventional synthetic datasets (Roberts et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2023), including SynthVerse (Zhao et al., 2026), often depend on manually constructed environments, constraining visual diversity and scalability. Recent gameplay datasets offer richer environments but remain limited in supervision. SeKai-Game (Li et al., 2026b) lacks depth annotations, while OmniWorld-Game (Zhou et al., 2025) relies on 𝜋3estimated (Wang et al., 2026b) camera trajectories rather than ground truth. Neither provides synchronized multi-view observations or audio, highlighting the need for unified, scalable dataset with diverse environments, rich multimodal supervision, and flexible view configurations to advance both visual generation and geometric learning. *Corresponding authors. 2026 Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. All rights reserved. Figure 1. GameRealm overview. GameRealm spans diverse games and supports multiple tasks: single-view, multi-view, and panoramic world modeling, alongside stereo, multi-view reconstruction, and point tracking. The collage showcases original game ground-truth data totaling over 120 million frames and 1,000 hours. To address these limitations, we introduce GameRealm, large-scale game-derived dataset that integrates geometric ground truth, synchronized multimodal signals, and diverse visual observations across single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic configurations. GameRealm comprises over 120 million frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay across diverse environments and interaction scenarios. We combine human-operated collection to capture diverse and context-dependent interactions with automated exploration to systematically navigate free-roaming environments. Through dedicated game-engine plugins, our acquisition pipeline directly accesses ground truth, establishing precise correspondence between visual observations and their underlying geometric and control information. The collected data include synchronized RGB images, metric depth, camera parameters, audio, keyboard and mouse inputs, and point tracking. Furthermore, we filter visually degraded and inconsistent clips. On the other hand, we examine the utility of GameRealm through multiple visual learning tasks. Employing the recorded player inputs, we fine-tune the world model to predict how the players view evolves under sequence of keyboard and mouse commands. We then study the geometric information in these recordings by fine-tuning models for stereo reconstruction and multi-view reconstruction. Evaluation on public real-world benchmarks tests how well the geometric supervision acquired in games transfers beyond the environments in which it was collected. Our contributions are as follows: We introduce GameRealm, large-scale game-derived dataset featuring 110M+ frames, 1,000+ hours of gameplay, synchronized multimodal ground truth, and diverse viewing configurations. We develop an game-grounded acquisition pipeline, integrating human interaction, agentic exploration, and multi-view-aware quality assessment for scalable and reliable data collection. We validate GameRealm across diverse downstream tasks, spanning interactive world modeling and geometric reconstruction, demonstrating its versatility and cross-domain generalization. We propose point tracking benchmark for 2D and 3D point tracking across diverse motions, 2 targets, and environments, with eight subcategories grouped under Interaction and Locomotion. 2. Related Work 2.1. Datasets Synthetic datasets provide geometric and motion supervision at scale. MPI Sintel (Butler et al., 2012b), Spring (Mehl et al., 2023), and Dynamic Replica (Karaev et al., 2023) support optical flow, stereo, and dynamic scene understanding, while TartanAir (Wang et al., 2020), BlendedMVS (Yao et al., 2020), Hypersim (Roberts et al., 2021), and EDEN (Le et al., 2021) target scene geometry and navigation. For temporal correspondence, FlyingThings++ (Harley et al., 2022) and PointOdyssey (Zheng et al., 2023) provide point-tracking supervision. Recent datasets, including Syn4D (Jiang et al., 2026) and SynthVerse (Zhao et al., 2026), further extend synthetic data toward synchronized multi-view observations, dense 4D correspondence, and diverse interactions.

Comparison between Gamerealm and existing synthetic datasets. Game-derived datasets offer complementary source of realistic visual observations and interactive supervision. Sekai-Game (Li et al., 2026b) provides gameplay videos with engine-derived camera trajectories, while OmniWorld-Game (Zhou et al., 2025) combines renderer-derived depth with estimated camera poses and generated annotations. Despite these advances, existing resources provide limited combinations of multi-view observations, audio, and recorded control inputs. Moreover, estimated annotations and camera trajectories do not provide the same supervision as game-native ground truth and actual player actions. As summarized in Table 1, GameRealm brings these capabilities together through synchronized RGB, metric depth, camera parameters, control inputs, audio, and point trajectories across single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic settings. Its acquisition pipeline combines human-operated interaction capture with automated exploration, providing unified resource for interactive world modeling and visual geometry learning. 2.2. Interactive World Model Interactive world models extend video generation to action-conditioned prediction of dynamic environments. Genie (Bruce et al., 2024) learns latent actions from unlabeled videos, while DIAMOND (Alonso et al., 2024) and GameNGen (Valevski et al., 2025) demonstrate diffusion-based and autoregressive approaches to interactive visual simulation. More recent methods, including Matrix-Game (Zhang et al., 2025b) and Matrix-Game 2.0 (He et al., 2025), introduce explicit keyboard and mouse condi3 tioning for controllable, real-time gameplay generation. These works establish actionobservation alignment as key requirement for interactive world modeling. Beyond short-term action following, recent methods focus on long-horizon consistency and persistent spatial memory. WorldPlay (Sun et al., 2025) employs reconstructed context memory, while LingBot-World 2.0 (Gao et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026b), AlayaWorld (Team et al., 2026a), and ReWorld (Chen et al., 2026) explore causal generation, compressed history, and geometry-aware memory for extended interaction. Meanwhile, panoramic world models such as PanoWorld (Li et al., 2026a) address spatial continuity under omnidirectional viewing, and LTX-2 (HaCohen et al., 2026) jointly generates synchronized video and audio. Together, these advances extend world modeling toward controllable, spatially consistent, and multimodal generation. GameRealm complements these model-centric advances with synchronized, engine-grounded supervision. It records visual observations alongside available player inputs, camera parameters, depth, and audio, enabling the adaptation of pretrained models such as Helios (Yuan et al., 2026) and LTX-2.3 to action-conditioned perspective and panoramic generation. This explicitly connects interactive generation with geometric and multimodal information. 2.3. Visual Geometry Grounded Learning Visual geometry learning aims to recover scene structure and motion from visual observations (Miao et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025b, 2026a). We focus on three complementary tasks: stereo reconstruction, multi-view reconstruction, and point tracking, which respectively recover depth, spatial structure, and persistent temporal correspondences. 2.3.1. Stereo Reconstruction Stereo reconstruction estimates dense disparity from calibrated image pairs and converts it into metric depth. Early learning-based methods, such as RAFT-Stereo (Lipson et al., 2021) and IGEVStereo (Xu et al., 2023), improve correspondence estimation through recurrent refinement and explicit geometric encoding. Recent approaches further incorporate monocular priors to handle ambiguous regions: Stereo Anywhere (Bartolomei et al., 2025), MonSter (Cheng et al., 2025), and DEFOMStereo (Jiang et al., 2025) combine stereo matching with pretrained visual or depth representations. FoundationStereo (Wen et al., 2025) and Fast-FoundationStereo (Wen et al., 2026) extend this direction toward robust zero-shot generalization and real-time inference. 2.3.2. Multi-view Reconstruction Traditional structure-from-motion and multi-view stereo methods (Schonberger and Frahm, 2016; Schönberger et al., 2016) recover camera poses and geometry through feature matching and geometric optimization. Recent feed-forward models simplify this process: DUSt3R (Wang et al., 2024) and MASt3R (Leroy et al., 2024) establish pairwise geometric reconstruction, while Fast3R (Yang et al., 2025), CUT3R (Wang et al., 2025c), and VGGT (Wang et al., 2025b, 2026a) extend reconstruction to multiple views and online perception. More recent models, including 𝜋3 (Wang et al., 2026b), MapAnything (Keetha et al., 2026), and Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2025), further improve flexibility across input configurations and geometric representations. Nevertheless, robustness to dynamic scenes, complex motion, and domain shifts remains challenging. GameRealm provides synchronized multi-view observations, metric depth, and per-frame camera parameters for geometric learning. We investigate their value by fine-tuning pretrained 𝜋3 model while retaining its original objectives and evaluation protocol, isolating the contribution of game-derived supervision to cross-domain reconstruction. 4 2.3.3. Point Tracking Point tracking establishes persistent correspondences across video frames under camera motion, occlusion, and object deformation. 2D methods such as TAPIR (Doersch et al., 2023) and CoTracker3 (Karaev et al., 2025) improve point localization and temporal consistency, while recent 3D trackers explicitly model scene geometry and camera motion. SpatialTrackerV2 (Xiao et al., 2025) jointly estimates 3D trajectories and camera motion, whereas TAPIP3D (Zhang et al., 2025a) tracks points in persistent 3D space. Correspondingly, TAPVid-3D (Koppula et al., 2024) and SynthVerse (Zhao et al., 2026) provide real-world and synthetic benchmarks for 3D tracking. Unlike projected 2D trajectories, world-space point positions provide direct supervision for separating object motion from camera motion. GameRealm records synchronized 3D point positions, 2D projections, depth, and camera parameters where supported by the acquisition pipeline, enabling the study of point tracking under diverse interactions and viewpoint changes. 3. GameRealm Dataset 3.1. Data Acquisition We develop unified game-data collection pipeline that integrates human-driven and automated data acquisition, as illustrated in Fig. 2. For interaction-rich scenarios, human operators provide direct control to capture complex interactions, while free-roaming scenarios are handled by an automated navigation system with frontier-based exploration and adaptive replanning. An agentic supervisor further monitors the automated process, detecting anomalies and triggering restarts when necessary. Data collected through both pathways undergo unified quality assessment and filtering to ensure consistency and reliability. The resulting dataset provides synchronized, game-native multimodal ground truth, including multi-view RGB images, metric depth, camera parameters, audio, keyboard and mouse inputs, and point tracking, supporting diverse downstream spatial understanding tasks. Figure 2. Data acquisition pipeline 3.1.1. Data Collection We implement dedicated game-engine plugin that provides direct access to engine-level ground-truth (GT) information, supporting two complementary acquisition paradigms, as shown in Fig. 3 (a): human-driven collection for gameplay involving complex, context-sensitive interactions, and automated collection for free-roaming scenarios that benefit from systematic navigation and exploration. 5 Ground-Truth Acquisition. The plugin directly captures game-native metric depth and camera parameters, following established practices in datasets such as TartanAir (Wang et al., 2020), and SeKai-Game (Li et al., 2026b). Game-engine timestamps ensure temporal synchronization across modalities and viewpoints. We evaluate cross-view alignment on view pairs randomly sampled from GameRealm clips and report the reprojection errors in Tab. 6. Human Collection. Human-operated collection primarily targets games with rich, context-dependent interactions. Representative activities include performing extreme-sports maneuvers, aiming and firing weapons, traversing complex terrain, and picking up or manipulating objects. These activities often require precise timing, coordinated controls, and context-aware decisions. Human operators execute meaningful gameplay sequences while the acquisition system records the corresponding observations and keyboard and mouse inputs. The resulting recordings follow the same unified ground-truth representation as automated collection, enabling both sources to be integrated into common dataset. Automated Collection. Automated collection primarily targets free-roaming games, where navigation provides practical means of acquiring diverse scene observations. The collection workflow consists of navigation queries, frontier selection, automatic navigation, and synchronized capture. Gamenative navigation queries identify reachable candidate destinations, and frontier selection prioritizes endpoints that extend spatial exploration. closed-loop controller then updates keyboard and mouse inputs according to the players position and route progress. Movement stalls trigger route replanning to support continued exploration. Figure 3. Data collection. GameRealm encompasses diverse game environments, firstand thirdperson perspectives, and wide range of playable characters, including humans and animals. Data are acquired through two complementary strategies: human-driven collection for interaction-rich scenarios (top) and automated collection for free-roaming scenarios (bottom) During navigation, the acquisition system records multi-view RGB-D together with frame-aligned 6 inputs. Timestamps are recorded for each captured observation and its corresponding inputs, enabling temporal synchronization across RGB images, depth maps, camera parameters, and control signals. An agentic supervisor is integrated into the automated collection workflow. It monitors runtime status, detects operational anomalies, and initiates restart procedures when needed. Its role is to manage collection failures, while navigation queries and the feedback controller govern gameplay movement. 3.2. Data Quality Assessment We first validate video integrity and motion consistency, as illustrated in Fig. 3 (b). All expected views must be present, and each video is fully decoded to verify its frame count, spatial dimensions, and frame rate against the corresponding annotations and acquisition settings. Groups with missing views or failed integrity checks are excluded. We then resize video frames to unified resolution and sample them at fixed intervals to estimate dense Farnebäck optical flow. For each sampled frame pair, we compute the spatially averaged flow magnitude and normalize it by the shorter image dimension. Clips with insufficient temporal motion or an excessively high ratio of maximum to mean motion magnitude, potentially indicating residual scene cuts or transitions, are excluded. We assess visual quality using complementary image-based and video-based predictors. Aesthetic Predictor V2.5, built on SigLIP encoder, scores frames sampled at one frame per second; their mean provides the aesthetic score 𝐴𝑣 for view 𝑣. DOVER++ (Wu et al., 2023), in turn, evaluates the video through technical and aesthetic quality branches. The branch outputs are calibrated, combined, and passed through sigmoid to obtain the video quality score 𝑄𝑣 in (0, 1). Both scores are stored for each view and used jointly in the subsequent selection step. Furthermore, selection operates on complete multi-view groups. In contrast, rejected clips suffer from severe exposure abnormalities, visual distortions caused by abnormal in-game character states (e.g., poisoning), or substantial view occlusions that obscure scene content. These examples illustrate how the filtering pipeline removes visually degraded samples while preserving informative and temporally consistent observations for downstream spatial understanding and learning tasks. 3.3. Data Annotation Unlike conventional video datasets that rely on vision-based algorithms to estimate geometric and motion annotations, GameRealm obtains ground-truth information directly from game engines through dedicated acquisition plugins. These plugins provide access to game-native information associated with game execution, enabling the collection of synchronized visual observations and corresponding geometric and control annotations. This acquisition paradigm establishes direct correspondence between rendered observations and their underlying engine-provided information, including depth, camera parameters, player inputs, and 3D point trajectories. All annotations are associated through engine-provided timestamps, ensuring temporal synchronization across modalities. Furthermore, geometric annotations follow consistent metric units and coordinate conventions, facilitating unified spatial interpretation across different data modalities. Consequently, GameRealm provides engine-grounded supervision without relying on post-hoc visual estimation for these annotations. Textual descriptions are generated separately using vision-language models and are distinguished from game-native annotations. 8 RGB observations. RGB observations are organized by recording, segment, and camera, with multi-view videos sharing common local frame index and retaining source-frame boundaries. Representative sequences have resolution of 1280 720, with corresponding depth maps, camera parameters, and available control inputs aligned to the exported timeline. Depth maps.Depth annotations provide numerical depth information in multiple formats, accompanied by corresponding decoding rules and invalid-value conventions. Metric depth, coordinate alignment, pixel registration, and annotation validity are documented and aligned according to the specifications of each data release. Camera Parameter.Camera annotations provide 3 3 intrinsic matrices and 4 4 camera-to-world transformations for supported sequences. Coordinate conventions, rotation composition, unit conversion, and synchronization information are documented for each data release, including explicit transformation Audio.Audio annotations include 48 kHz, two-channel WAV recordings, together with associated temporal and segment-level metadata. Audio availability, completeness, and temporal synchronization are documented individually for each recording. Keypress.Input annotations include keyboard and mouse states, such as directional keys, Space, and mouse buttons, with binary down and changed flags representing held states and state transitions. Where available, relative mouse displacements and frame-aligned timestamps are also retained to establish explicit temporal correspondence between user inputs and visual observations. Point tracking. Point annotations represent persistent correspondences through triangle addresses and barycentric coordinates or vertex identities, providing world-space 3D positions and per-view 2D projections where available. Visibility, synchronization, point identity, and geometric validity are documented according to annotation readiness, with additional skeletal joints and skinned vertices available for selected hand sequences. Video Caption. We construct hierarchical textual annotations for synchronized multi-view gameplay clips using Qwen3.5-Flash (Team, 2026), as illustrated in Fig. 2 (c). For each view, up to 200 frames are sampled after cropping and resizing, with original frame indices preserved. The model independently generates temporally ordered action descriptions covering entities, actions, spatial relationships, Figure 6. Data distribution Figure 7. Data composition and state changes. These descriptions are concatenated into local captions and subsequently fused through text-only call into shared global caption, prioritizing the primary view while incorporating compatible information from other views. Both caption types are validated and retained separately for downstream textual conditioning. 3.4. Data Statistics Data scale and modality coverage. GameRealm contains over 120 million RGB frames. Following Syn4D (Jiang et al., 2026) and SynthVerse (Zhao et al., 2026), we count synchronized frames from different cameras separately. Based on typical recording rates of 1624 fps, we estimate over 1,000 hours of video summed across all views. Each RGB frame is paired with metric depth map and camera parameters. Multi-view and panoramic sequences also include synchronized audio and action annotations, providing multimodal supervision for interactive world modeling. Fig. 6 shows the frame distribution across more than 50 games. The number of frames collected per game depends on the size of its playable maps, with larger game worlds generally contributing more frames. Data composition. The dataset is predominantly composed of multi-view data (77.6%), followed by stereo (9.2%), panoramic (7.5%), and single-view data (5.7%). The dominance of multi-view data reflects our acquisition design, which prioritizes synchronized multi-camera capture to provide broader spatial coverage and richer geometric supervision across diverse game environments. Stereo, panoramic, and single-view data are collected as complementary configurations for specific visual learning tasks. Within the tracking subset, multi-view and single-view observations account for 63.9% and 36.1%, respectively. Among samples with explicit perspective annotations, first-person and third-person views constitute 45.6% and 54.4%, respectively, indicating relatively balanced representation of the two perspectives. GameRealm encompasses diverse game content across four semantic dimensions: scene, weather, character, and interaction, as summarized in Fig. 6 . These dimensions capture complementary aspects of gameplay, including environmental conditions, spatial settings, agent behaviors, and entity types. Fig. 910 present representative examples of these categories, illustrating the diversity of visual content covered by our data acquisition pipeline. Scene diversity. Figure 8 illustrates the broad range of environments represented in GameRealm, spanning natural scenes such as forests, grasslands, mountains, deserts, rivers, lakes, beaches, underwater environments, and caves, as well as human-made settings such as urban streets, villages, and laboratories. This diversity encompasses different spatial layouts, geometric structures, and visual characteristics, enabling the study of scene understanding and geometric learning across heterogeneous environments. Weather diversity. As shown in Fig. 9, GameRealm covers variety of weather conditions and times 10 Figure 8. Scene. The first row shows human-oriented environments, including indoor spaces, urban streets, and outer space, while the second row presents natural environments such as snowfields, forests, lava fields, and lakes. of day, including sunny, cloudy, rainy, snowy, foggy, and stormy environments, as well as variations in daylight and illumination. These conditions introduce visual changes in scene appearance, lighting, visibility, and atmospheric effects, providing diverse environmental contexts for learning robust visual representations and modeling dynamic worlds. Figure 9. Weather. The first row illustrates weather conditions, including rain, snow, and fog, while the second row shows the progression of time from pre-dawn and morning through noon, dusk, and late night. Character diversity. Figure 10 demonstrates the diversity of entities appearing in GameRealm, including humans, robots, cats, canines, birds, sharks, ants, beetles, spiders, and monsters. These entities exhibit different appearances, shapes, scales, and motion characteristics, broadening the range of visual and dynamic patterns represented in the dataset. Combined with the diversity of scenes and interactions, this variety supports the evaluation of world models and visual understanding methods across different characters and gameplay contexts. Figure 10. Character. Representative examples of character diversity in GameRealm, including robots, fish, birds, dragons, humans, and many others. Interaction diversity. As illustrated in Fig. 11, GameRealm captures wide range of gameplay activities, including roaming, walking, running, jumping, climbing, swimming, aiming, shooting, 11 blocking, dodging, driving, riding, boating, skiing, and object-related operations such as picking, placing, opening, closing, folding, and removing. These activities introduce varied motion patterns and interaction dynamics, supporting the investigation of action-conditioned world modeling and the representation of dynamic scenes under different control inputs. Figure 11. Interaction. Representative interaction activities in GameRealm, including motorcycle riding, driving, skiing, opening doors, jumping, and other diverse gameplay interactions. 4. Interactive World Model We evaluate GameRealm for interactive world modeling by adapting pretrained generative models with LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) and lightweight conditioning modules. We investigate three settings: singleview action-conditioned generation, synchronized multi-view generation, and panoramic audio-visual generation. Figure 12. As illustrated in Fig. 12, we adapt the pretrained 40-block Helios backbone. Quantitative results We evaluate the effectiveness of GameRealms action annotations for interactive world modeling using VBench++ (Huang et al., 2025) and iWorld-Bench (Fang et al., 2026). As 13 shown in Tab. 2, the fine-tuned Helios maintains visual quality and motion stability under zero-action conditions. We further assess directional controllability across eight inputs, including WASD movement and joystick-based viewpoint control (up, down, left, and right). As shown in Tab. 3, Helios achieves direction success rate of 76.59%, demonstrating that GameRealms action annotations provide effective supervision for learning controllable visual dynamics. Compared with the reference models, our method produces more spatially distributed reconstructions, with successive subject observations more clearly separated along the visible path. 5.4. Point Tracking GameRealm supports both the evaluation and learning of point tracking. TrajRealm-Bench measures correspondence across diverse interactions and locomotion, while fine-tuning experiments with TAPIP3D (Zhang et al., 2025a) and TrackEverything (Jain et al., 2026) assess transfer to synthetic environments and real-world video. Evaluation metrics and input conditions. Following TAPIP3D, SynthVerse, and TAPVid-3D (Koppula et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2026), evaluation reports average Jaccard (AJ), average percentage of points within distance thresholds (APD), and occlusion accuracy (OA). AJ jointly measures localization and visibility; APD averages localization accuracy across five thresholds; OA measures visibility classification accuracy. The benchmark and synthetic experiments report 3D and projected 2D AJ/APD together with OA; real-world evaluation reports AJ3𝐷, APD3𝐷, and OA. All scores are percentages, with higher values indicating better performance. Benchmark methods are grouped by whether the complete tracking pipeline uses ground-truth (GT) depth and camera poses, including 3D lifting and coordinate conversion. MoSE3 (Cheng et al., 2026), Track4World (Lu et al., 2026), and TrackEverything+𝜋3 (Jain et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b) use estimated geometry. CoTracker2.1 (Karaev et al., 2024), CoTracker3 (Karaev et al., 2025), DELTA (Ngo et al., 2025), SpatialTrackerV2 (Xiao et al., 2025), TAPIP3D, and TrackEverything+GT use GT geometry. CoTracker predicts image-space tracks and uses GT depth and poses for 3D lifting. The With GT group uses median scale normalization and depth-adaptive 3D thresholds. The Without GT group follows the MoSE3 protocol: first-frame camera coordinates, global L1 scale and translation fitting, second median rescaling, and fixed 3D thresholds. Neither group fits rotation. Comparisons 23 therefore use consistent scoring within each group. Proposed point tracking benchmark. TrajRealm-Bench contains 175 sequences and 104,306 camera frames across eight subsets  (Table 9)  . Interaction evaluates point identity through contact, articulation, and occlusion: General covers everyday human, animal, and object interactions; Hard covers rapid motion and large pose changes; Embodied covers robotic manipulation; and Plant covers deforming leaves and branches. Locomotion evaluates movement through environments: General covers individual movement and navigation; Transportation covers driving and riding; Group covers intersecting trajectories and mutual occlusion; and Long-horizon covers sustained movement over more than 800 temporal frames. Each sequence belongs to one subset, with Long-horizon sequences assigned exclusively to that subset. Recording-group splits keep synchronized views and adjacent windows together. Evaluation retains full sequences, with up to 256 unique annotated queries per camera input, initialized at their first eligible visible frame. The 191 camera inputs provide 42,173 queries. AJ and OA use fixed visibility threshold of 0.5 on this benchmark. Scores are averaged across views within each source sequence and then across sequences within each subset; family and overall averages weight their four and eight subsets equally. CoTracker2.1, DELTA, and TAPIP3D use 16-frame windows with stride 8; SpatialTrackerV2 uses length/stride 200/196 offline and 20/14 online; TrackEverything uses 16/16 blocks with persistent scene memory; CoTracker3-offline processes the full sequence jointly. TrackEverything+𝜋3 estimates geometry in 60-frame chunks with overlap 30. Table 9. Proposed benchmark statistics.

Conclusion In this work, we introduced GameRealm, large-scale game-derived dataset that grounds visual observations in ground-truth geometric and interactive information. By combining human-operated interaction capture with agentic automated exploration, GameRealm provides diverse and synchronized multimodal data across multiple viewing configurations. We further establish scalable acquisition and quality assessment pipeline to ensure data integrity and cross-view consistency. Experiments across multiple representative visual learning tasks demonstrate its utility for interactive world modeling and visual geometry learning, with promising results in action-conditioned generation and cross-domain geometric generalization. In future work, we aim to enrich GameRealm with finergrained ground-truth annotations, including human and object skeletons, pixel-level segmentation masks, and instance-level information, to support broader range of visual learning tasks.
